source.title: Approximate Fisher Information Matrix to Characterize the Training of Deep Neural Networks
source.authors: Zhi-Bin Liao; T. Drummond; I. Reid; G. Carneiro

record.file_problem: The full paper and supplementary material are present; no relevant section appears cut off or garbled.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares held-out errors and training errors across mini-batch sizes and learning rates, and tests dynamic batch schedules using a different training setup from the claim versions’ cited studies.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results for batch size and learning rate, including training and testing errors, and evaluates dynamic sampling. Its discussions of prior work on sharp minima and generalization are citations, not this study’s results. Rows below retain the highlighted CIFAR-10 fixed-batch results and the reported dynamic-sampling CIFAR-10 ResNet comparison; the supplementary material contains many additional configurations.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own held-out errors across batch sizes and learning rates at fixed epoch budgets, and compares fixed batches with dynamic batch schedules. These results test V5. Its Fisher measures do not measure V7's magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance or generalization-gap ranking.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate. The authors conclude that their two Fisher-derived measurements help characterize convergence and generalization across batch sizes and learning rates, and can guide dynamic sampling toward faster training with competitive accuracy. They present empirical evidence and potential predictive utility, not a demonstrated universal guarantee.
record.recipe_differences: Uses SGD with momentum and batch-size/learning-rate sweeps, but adds Fisher-derived measures and dynamic sampling; all experiments use data augmentation. It does not test random-label memorization.
record.method_sensitivity: Testing error varies with mini-batch size and initial learning rate; the authors also report different outcomes for increasing versus decreasing batch schedules and for multi-step versus whole-run dynamic sampling.

fits_no_version.finding: Approximate Fisher conditioning and learning-rate-weighted cumulative energy jointly characterize convergence and testing error across the sweeps; neither is magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Joint Fisher-derived conditioning and energy measurements can characterize training outcomes and guide batch-size scheduling.

record.peer_reviewed: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
record.problems: The paper uses data augmentation throughout and reports means over five independently trained models. Its reported generalization comparisons do not isolate batch size from learning rate; the authors explicitly state these effects interact. DenseNet batch size 512 was excluded because it could not be trained on a single GPU. The supplement’s flattened tables make many cell-to-condition assignments difficult to reconstruct beyond the values retained here.
record.rows_left_out: The supplementary material reports many additional fixed-batch testing and training error cells across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SVHN, MNIST, and an MLP, plus more dynamic schedules in Table 1 and training-error tables. Only highlighted CIFAR-10 fixed-batch results and the CIFAR-10 ResNet dynamic-schedule comparisons were retained; the remaining cells were omitted because the full sweep exceeds the 60-row limit and the supplied flattened tables make some assignments difficult to verify.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and the natural-label versus random-label held-out comparison.
Width sweeps beyond the width required for zero training error.

An interpretable convolutional versus fully connected comparison and the contribution of local connectivity. The separate MLP illustration does not isolate architecture, and its supplementary training and testing tables repeat identical values.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD, tuning breadth, decoupled weight decay, and optimizer switching.

Language workloads, longer-training interventions, warmup, and normalization or regularization interventions. Dynamic batch scheduling is tested, but a standalone learning-rate scaling rule is not isolated.
Dropout interventions, training-set-size dependence, and joint removal of dropout and weight decay.
Magnitude-scaled weight perturbations, their association with the training–test gap at similarly low training loss, and comparisons against norm- and margin-based measures.
Removal of memorized examples versus random removal.

record.verdict_notes: Only V5 receives verdicts. Additional fixed-batch sweeps, training errors, and dynamic schedules are already declared in rows_left_out, so they are not listed as missing. The Table 1 p-value misattribution affects R17 and R19, not their supplementary error values. Small-batch reference rows remain linked to V5 but do not independently establish its effect. All comparisons use augmentation and five independently initialized runs.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label training or comparison with natural labels.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison on images.

The fixed-batch comparisons vary batch size and learning rate over a fixed training duration, but do not characterize a workload-dependent critical batch size. Dynamic sampling is tested, but the stated controls involving normalization or regularization changes are not.

The study measures approximate Fisher condition number and cumulative energy against generalization, not magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness or the norm- and margin-based measures named in the version.

rows.subject: ResNet dynamic-sampling model s32-to-512
rows.operation_detail: Dynamic sampling changes batch size over five equal-duration training stages.
rows.note: The study reports this schedule has similar classification accuracy to the beacon models, but the multi-step variant performs better in this comparison.
rows.check: The 5.07% ± 0.21% value is correct, but Table 1's p=0.029 compares s32-to-128 with s32-to-128-MS, not this pair. Relevant fixed-batch references are R2, 4.78%, and R8, 6.55%: dynamic sampling reduces but does not numerically eliminate the penalty.

source_check.correct: s32-to-512: 5.07% ± 0.21%; s32-to-512-MS: 4.97% ± 0.13%. Their comparison has no reported p-value. Table 1's p=0.029 compares s32-to-128, 4.90% ± 0.05%, with s32-to-128-MS, 4.76% ± 0.13%.
source_check.locator_found: Section 4.3, p. 9; Table 1, p. 10, CIFAR-10 ResNet columns; supplementary material, p. 17, dynamic-sampling testing errors.
source_check.problem: The reported p=0.029 belongs to a different schedule pair.

rows.subject: ResNet dynamic-sampling model s512-to-32
rows.operation_detail: Dynamic sampling decreases batch size over five equal-duration training stages.
rows.note: The paper reports these two schedules use the same amount of mini-batch sizes and have statistically different test results.
rows.check: The value and p=0.0037 comparison are supported by section 4.3. Add fixed-batch references R2 and R8: error 5.56% lies between their 4.78% and 6.55%. The comparison with R17 shows schedule-order dependence, not an isolated fixed-batch effect.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4.3, p. 9, comparison of s32-to-512 and s512-to-32; supplementary material, p. 17.
